title: Quantitative photoconversion analysis of internal molecular dynamics in stress granules
author: Amen, Kaganovich
materials: We followed standard cell culturing protocols for all experiments. HEK293T cells modified via CRISPR-Cas9 were maintained in the DMEM (Pan Biotech) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1% penicillin/streptomycin, at 37°C/5% CO2. Puromycin (2 μg/mL, Sigma) selection can be omitted after a clonal endogenously tagged population was obtained and verified.Alternatives: Some imaging systems are sensitive to the media composition. If your microscope detects the signal from phenol red in the media, use phenol red free alternatives. Additionally, if your microscope is not equipped with a CO2 chamber, you can replace the media with a HEPES pH7.4 containing media.4.One day before the experiment split the cells into a glass-bottom imaging plate. We use a 4-well 35 mm plates (Cellvis).Note: Splitting a day before the experiment allows the cells to recover. Adjust the timing of splitting according to your cell line. The goal here is to have a healthy cell line. Some cells, like stem cells, will require glass coating with an appropriate coating layer, e.g., Matrigel (Corning Life Sciences). You can choose to use a separate plate for each treatment, however having treatments in separate wells of the same plate consumes less time per repeat.

steps.title: Prepare cell culture for imaging
steps.instruction: Maintain CRISPR‑edited HEK293T cells in DMEM (Pan Biotech) supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum and 1 % penicillin/streptomycin at 37 °C and 5 % CO₂. Add puromycin at 2 µg mL⁻¹ (Sigma) only if a clonal endogenously tagged population has not yet been verified; otherwise omit. If the microscope detects phenol red, switch to phenol‑red‑free medium, and if no CO₂ chamber is available, replace the medium with HEPES‑buffered (pH 7.4) formulation. One day before imaging, split the cells onto a glass‑bottom 4‑well 35 mm plate (Cellvis), allowing recovery; coat the glass with Matrigel (Corning Life Sciences) for stem‑like cells if needed.

steps.title: Set up microscope environmental controls
steps.instruction: Power on the Nikon A1r confocal microscope, ensure the CO₂ and temperature control units (OKO Lab) are running, and wait until CO₂ and temperature are stabilized before placing the plate on the stage. Visually inspect cells for health and confirm media pH by checking color (if phenol red is present).

steps.title: Photoconvert target region with 406 nm laser
steps.instruction: Configure the microscope for bi‑directional resonant scanning at 512 × 512 pixels. Select the 406 nm laser (Coherent, 50 mW) and set it to 10 % of maximum power, delivering 100 ms pulses. Perform a test run to verify conversion efficiency and adjust pulse duration or power as needed; multiple pulses may be applied to cover the desired portion of the membraneless compartment.

steps.title: Configure imaging for photoconverted proteins
steps.instruction: Switch to slower, higher‑resolution galvanometer scanning mode. Install the CFI Plan Apo Lambda 60× oil immersion objective. Set the 488 nm laser (Coherent, 50 mW) and the 561 nm laser (Coherent, 50 mW) to the appropriate power for imaging the photoconverted signal.

steps.title: Acquire time‑lapse images of photoconverted area
steps.instruction: Begin recording movies of the photoconverted region using the settings defined above, ensuring sufficient temporal resolution to capture protein diffusion dynamics.

steps.title: Quantify diffusion time from intensity profiles
steps.instruction: For each movie, plot the fluorescence intensity of the photoconverted region and of adjacent non‑converted areas. Define the diffusion time as the first time point when the mean intensity of the photoconverted area equals that of the adjacent area within a 5 % margin.

steps.title: Perform statistical analysis of diffusion data
steps.instruction: Exclude movies that lost focus or showed drastic organelle shape changes. Test the remaining diffusion times for normality with the Shapiro‑Wilk test and for equal variances with Levene’s test. Compute significance using a two‑tailed Student’s t‑test for two‑condition comparisons or one‑way ANOVA for more than two conditions.
